"Hey man, is your name Dante?" a voice is asking.

You sit up with a start. "Yeah."

The attic is different now but you couldn't say why. How. You don't know how 
it's different. You're sitting on the floor -- lying on it, more accurately -- 
and for a split second, everything's slowed down and peaceful and makes sense, 
even the Easy-Bake oven.

Then this guy with a dirty baseball cap (what the fuck? how cliched are we 
going to get tonight?) who's been standing over you has to start talking to you 
again and it fucks everything up. No sign of your esteemed drug merchant, of 
course. He's probably onto bigger and better prey.

"There's this girl who's been calling everyone's cell phones asking for you, 
man."

You frown.

"Here, talk to her, man, she's been freaking out on me the last fifteen 
minutes."

He presses his cell phone up to your ear, which is a nice thing to do 
considering your arms are completely numb for reasons you don't want to think 
about right now.

"Dante?" asks a voice you recognize in an instant, never mind the cell phone, 
never mind the years: it's Beatrice. If this were a movie, there'd be a 
convenient fade to black to allow you to reminisce about your shared past 
history, perhaps beginning with that sunrise six years ago -- but this isn't a 
movie, kiddo, and she says again:

"Dante, is that you?"

She's crying.

events.response:
Of course you remember where her fucking house is. You still remember every 
single thing about her. French toast for breakfast with enough syrup to drown 
yourself...

"It's important," Beatrice says. "Come as soon as you can."

There's a faint click, like a bird's beak tapping on a chalkboard, and then she 
isn't there anymore.

Your arms are working now -- you're pushing yourself up off the floor without 
even realizing it -- and so is your voice. "I've got to go see her," you're 
saying.

The guy with the cell phone gives you as serious a look as a frat boy can. 
"Dude, I've never met you before or anything, but can I give you some advice? 
If I were you, I wouldn't drive anywhere tonight? Not with the kind of pupils 
you've got."

He backs away from you, maybe waiting for a rebuttal. But there's no point in 
arguing with a frat boy who's managed to cobble together some kind of personal 
belief.

"Can you give me a ride?" you ask.

"Nah, man," he says, suddenly displaying an interest in the stairway. "I gotta 
get back downstairs. The dance won't dance itself, you know what I'm saying?"

If you were not at all on drugs right now, you'd be able to come up with a 
really killer line, but it doesn't matter. There's got to be somebody at this 
hoedown that can get you to Beatrice.

Not Exactly the Same Attic
It's the light that makes it different: somehow it's become even dimmer than 
before, so that everything is shadow but your own body and the stairs leading 
down. Who knows what's in the recesses of the dark? Probably plenty of useful 
things: things to keep your shoelaces tied, things to remind you of your 
dentist appointments -- even things that could save your own life. But who 
knows? It's just a pile of stuff you don't know how to sort through.

The music downstairs is insistent, even burning.

genetic instinct and secular humanism that no one's bumping into anyone else, 
except when they want to, which is always... Why don't you touch people more? 
You never hug people except when they hug you first. Your grandmother leaving 
for a trip to New Orleans, to see where her body will reside once she's gone up

support the White House's pediment? How long to pack all the sand as tight as a

sure it never falls?

The great iron doors of the White House are beneath the pediment to the east. 
If you'd like, you can also walk around the White House to the northeast and 
southeast.

here four years ago.

events.intent: Press Enter to continue the blue chair scene
events.response:
"Would you run in and grab me a doughnut?"

It hurts to wake up. You feel scared but don't know why. Your throat's dry, 
which always happens to you when you take a nap, and your arms hurt, which is 
new. You're not sure what to think, what to feel.

There's not much to see but you feel confused anyway. The car's parked beside a 
gas pump now, and there's a slight breeze coming through the window beside you. 
The air is just cold enough to be considered cool. Your eyes keep shifting over 
the same things, like you're going to catch something being wrong, being fake, 
being part of the dream still.

But you're awake. You really are.

"A doughnut?" you ask.

"Yeah, I gotta fill up the tank," Chris says. "If they have Krispy Kreme, that 
would be ideal."

He plops a couple wrinked bills in your hand and gets out of the car. You're 
still not sure what to do, but what the fuck? Start with something simple. 
Follow his lead, get out of the car. Standing up feels weird for half a second, 
like maybe you're going to faint but you've never fainted before or anything, 
it's just how you imagine it might feel. And then the feeling's gone.

You are awake. This is an important fact to remember -- you tell yourself this 
a couple times, to make sure it sinks in.

A Gas Station in the Middle of Nowhere
Everything's so fucking yellow, like you're a zombie now and your optic nerves 
have fermented or something. It's because of those stupid low-energy lights 
overhead. Saving the planet by turning it ugly. Goddammit -- your eyes hurt now.

No one else is here, but that kind of makes sense. You're not sure what time it 
is, but it must be late. The gas station's off some two-lane highway, but there 
aren't any road signs, so you have no idea where you are, either. But it 
doesn't really matter, you guess. Chris knows where to go -- you told him, 
after all.

There's a mini-mart to the east that looks open. Above it is a sign that reads 
LUCKY'S in kind-of shoddy painter's script.

Chris is occupied pumping gas -- he's humming this random sort of song to 
himself that you don't recognize.

events.intent: Look at the girl with the lantern who has now appeared in person
events.response:
Alice is good at waiting. This is a joke she tells herself and no one else; she 
works as a waitress in an Italian restaurant she would call "nice enough." So 
much of her life is nice enough. She went to a decent college -- not a state 
school, but not really prestigious, either. She tried to get into grad school, 
but she wasn't accepted anywhere.

The funny thing is it didn't feel bad to get all those rejection letters. She 
just moved on to what was possible. A small apartment and a small job. Not 
small -- nice enough. She doesn't feel bad. When she knows what she wants to 
be, she'll know.

faith?
